applies_to: Armstrong Monitoring AMC-1DBx digital gas detection controllers with up to 988 sensors, 256 relays, 128 zones and 128 analog outputs.
summary: The AMC-1DBx is a gas detection controller for large sensor networks. Over BACnet IP it exposes 4,119 fixed objects: a system state, then for each possible sensor a raw value, a cause state and a status string, and the same kind of blocks for relays, zones and analog outputs, plus file objects for logs, database and firmware. Configuration is not available over BACnet.
notes: Objects come in fixed instance ranges, one object per sensor, relay, zone or output. Only the first object of each range is listed; the range is in each description (e.g. AI 0-987 = sensors 1-988).
Object names are not printed; the group labels from the object list are used.
Analog outputs are Analog Input objects AI 988-1115. OctetString Value objects (OS) carry packed status bytes.
All objects are read-only except File objects; some support Out-Of-Service for testing interlocks.
Cause states are 6-bit masks reported as values 1-32, where 32 = All Clear.

source.title: Digital Monitor 1DBx Series BAS Interface Manual

integration.summary: Watch MSI 0 for the overall state (32 = All Clear; the Relay bit means an alarm event). Then read only the sensors, relays and zones actually installed, using the device counts in OS 0, rather than discovering all 4,119 objects. COV on the cause-state objects avoids heavy polling.
setup: BACnet IP only (MS/TP not available); default IP 10.0.0.103/24, router 10.0.0.1, UDP 47808 (47808-47823 allowed).
Default device ID 677003, network 0; BBMD address 0.0.0.0 when not used; BACnet IP time to live 60 s.
Settings are made in the monitor's Interface > BACnet menu.
gotchas: Full discovery of 4,119 objects can take many minutes; add only the objects for installed devices.
Up to 255 simultaneous confirmed COV messages; COV lists over 31 entries may cause segmentation aborts.
After IP or BACnet changes treat the monitor as unreliable for another 120 s once it answers again.
Writing push.fw or push.db starts a firmware or database update; never write those files casually.

points.name: System Status State
points.description: Monitor state, 6-bit mask: Failed, HourGlass, Relay, Acknowledge, PowerUp
points.states: 32 = All Clear; values 1-31 = bit mask [Failed, HourGlass, Relay, Acknowledge, PowerUp]

points.name: System Status Info.
points.description: 9-byte system info: state, DIP disables, delays, device counts

points.name: Sensors Raw Input
points.description: Sensor 001 raw value (AI 0-987 = sensors 1-988); 800-4000 mV = 0-100 % FS

points.name: Sensor Cause State
points.states: 32 = All Clear; values 1-31 = bit mask [Delay Timer, Fail, Alarm3, Alarm2, Alarm1]

points.name: Sensor Status Info.
points.description: Sensor 001 info (OS 1-988): availability, state, assigned relays

points.name: Relay Current Condition
points.description: Relay 001 condition (BI 0-255 = relays 1-256); read with Polarity

points.name: Relay Cause State
points.states: 32 = All Clear; values 1-31 = bit mask [Run Timer, Dew, Schedule, Zone, Sensor]

points.name: Relay Status Info.
points.description: Relay 001 info (OS 989-1244): availability, state, alarm counts, run timers

points.name: Zone Cause State
points.states: 32 = All Clear; values 1-31 = bit mask [Schedule, Fail, Alarm3, Alarm2, Alarm1]

points.name: Zone Status Info.
points.description: Zone 001 info (OS 1245-1372): availability, state, relays, analog output

points.name: RAM1:\push.fw

points.description: Command file: write to export the database
